items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we wish to evaluate [MATH: \log_{4}9,] but our calculator only has a key for the common logarithm [MATH: \log] (base [MATH: 10]).

Content:
In such cases, we can use the change of base formula, which states that
[MATH: \log_a X = \dfrac {\log_b X} {\log_b a}.]
It effectively allows us to change a logarithm from one base, [MATH: a,] to another, [MATH: b.] Note that [MATH: X,] [MATH: a,] and [MATH: b] have to be all greater than zero and that [MATH: a \ne 1,] [MATH: b \ne 1.]

Content:
Using this formula, we can rewrite the logarithm from base [MATH: a=4] to base [MATH: b=10,] to get
[MATH: \log_{4} 9|= (\log 9)/(\log 4); ≈ (0.954242)/(0.602059); = 1.585]
rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

items.title: Rewriting a Logarithm Using the Change of Base Formula

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following is equivalent to [MATH: \log x ?]

  1. [MATH: \dfrac {\log_{2} x} {\log_{2} 10}]

  2. [MATH: \dfrac {\log_{2} 10} {\log_{2} x}]

  3. [MATH: \log_{2}\left(\dfrac{x}{10}\right)]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following is equivalent to [MATH: \log x ?]

1. [MATH: \dfrac {\log_{2} x} {\log_{2} 10}]
2. [MATH: \dfrac {\log_{2} 10} {\log_{2} x}]
3. [MATH: \log_{2}\left(\dfrac{x}{10}\right)]

sections.normalized_html:
The change of base formula for logarithms is

[MATH: \log_a X = \dfrac {\log_b X} {\log_b a}.]

We want to change from base [MATH: a=10] to base [MATH: b=2.] Therefore, we have

[MATH: \log x|= \log_{10} x; = (\log_{2} x)/(\log_{2} 10).]

So, the correct answer is "I only."

2. [MATH: \dfrac {\log_{2} 10} {\log_{2} x}]

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The change of base formula for logarithms is

We want to change from base [MATH: a=10] to base [MATH: b=2.] Therefore, we have

[MATH: \log x|= \log_{10} x; = (\log_{2} x)/(\log_{2} 10).]

So, the correct answer is "I only."

sections.normalized_html:
Let's calculate [MATH: \log_3 (7)] by changing the base [MATH: 3] to the common logarithm (base [MATH: 10]).

We use the change of base formula: [MATH: \log_a X = \dfrac {\log_b X} {\log_b a}]

In our case, we have [MATH: a=3,] [MATH: X =7,] and [MATH: b=10.] So, we have

[MATH: \log_{3} (7)|= (\log_{10} (7))/(\log_{10} (3)); = (\log (7))/(\log (3)); ≈ (0.84510)/(0.47712); ≈ 1.77.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we wish to evaluate [MATH: \log_{4}9,] but our calculator only has a key for the common logarithm [MATH: \log] (base [MATH: 10]).

Content:
In such cases, we can use the change of base formula, which states that
[MATH: \log_a X = \dfrac {\log_b X} {\log_b a}.]
It effectively allows us to change a logarithm from one base, [MATH: a,] to another, [MATH: b.] Note that [MATH: X,] [MATH: a,] and [MATH: b] have to be all greater than zero and that [MATH: a \ne 1,] [MATH: b \ne 1.]

Content:
Using this formula, we can rewrite the logarithm from base [MATH: a=4] to base [MATH: b=10,] to get
[MATH: \log_{4} 9|= (\log 9)/(\log 4); ≈ (0.954242)/(0.602059); = 1.585]
rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

---

Item 2 — Example: Rewriting a Logarithm Using the Change of Base Formula

Example Prompt:
Which of the following is equivalent to [MATH: \log x ?]

1. [MATH: \dfrac {\log_{2} x} {\log_{2} 10}]
2. [MATH: \dfrac {\log_{2} 10} {\log_{2} x}]
3. [MATH: \log_{2}\left(\dfrac{x}{10}\right)]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The change of base formula for logarithms is

[MATH: \log_a X = \dfrac {\log_b X} {\log_b a}.]

We want to change from base [MATH: a=10] to base [MATH: b=2.] Therefore, we have

[MATH: \log x|= \log_{10} x; = (\log_{2} x)/(\log_{2} 10).]

So, the correct answer is "I only."

Let's calculate [MATH: \log_3 (7)] by changing the base [MATH: 3] to the common logarithm (base [MATH: 10]).

In our case, we have [MATH: a=3,] [MATH: X =7,] and [MATH: b=10.] So, we have

[MATH: \log_{3} (7)|= (\log_{10} (7))/(\log_{10} (3)); = (\log (7))/(\log (3)); ≈ (0.84510)/(0.47712); ≈ 1.77.]
